title: 3-Read Friday #33: Survivorship Bias, Memorisation, and Retrieval Buy-In
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue #33 links three posts on cognitive bias and revision strategy. Craig Latimir applies the WWII 'survivorship bias' story to education, arguing that teachers and leaders often assume structures and explicit instruction are unnecessary because they personally survived without them. Dylan Kane distinguishes worthwhile from wasteful memorisation in maths class. Peps McCrea highlights a study finding 45% of students still default to ineffective rereading and note-taking rather than retrieval practice when revising. Barton frames all three as timely reading heading into exam season.
points: Barton highlights Latimir's survivorship-bias framing as raising 'really important questions' about why teachers and leaders assume today's students don't need explicit structures they themselves never received.
He credits Kane with clarifying that 'memorisation' is a polarising but frequently misunderstood word, useful only when applied to knowledge worth committing to long-term memory.
He flags McCrea's citation of a study showing 45% of students rely predominantly on rereading and note-taking as 'a good one to share with students' before exams.
quotes: Craig takes the concept of survivorship bias (using the classic example of WW2 planes) and applies it to the word of education.
As teachers, we were never taught how to plan lessons, and we did okay, so why do we need to support other teachers in doing so?
As Dylan points out at the top of this post, the word 'memorisation' is polarising for teachers.
I love the link to the study that suggests 45% of students rely predominantly on rereading and note-taking when we know these are not as effective as practice testing and other retrieval strategies.
This is a good one to share with students in these last few weeks before exams!
